title: The prayer never stopped
hook: empires rose and fell, and the five prayers went on

segments.voice: Yesterday, one ummah: Bilal, Salman and Suhayb among the companions, and one row of many faces. Your line was many faces. What did you taste, hear or see from a culture new to you? Day one thousand fifty-five.

Try making a list of what's gone. The caliphs of Damascus. The caliphs of Baghdad. The courts of Cordoba and Cairo. Sultans, viziers, banners, coins with names nobody spends anymore. This path has spent a year watching them rise and fall. Now make the other list, of what's still here. It's shorter, and it's this: at dawn tomorrow, somewhere, someone will wash their face and hands and feet, stand on a mat, and say God is greatest. Then at noon. Then in the afternoon, at sunset, at night. The same five prayers people prayed under those rulers. Today: the prayer never stopped.
screen: `THE LIST OF WHAT'S GONE.` → `THE LIST OF WHAT'S STILL HERE.` → `FIVE TIMES, TOMORROW AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Why did the prayer outlast the empires? Start with how the Qur'an frames it. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours. Not tied to a palace, a capital or a king. Tied to the sun, which no dynasty owns. When a ruler fell, the sun still rose, and the time for dawn prayer still came. Second, the prayer was built not to stop. The Qur'an says that if you are in fear, you pray standing or on horseback, however you can, and when you're safe again you remember God as He taught you. Travelers shorten it. The sick pray sitting, or lying down. The form bends. The prayer doesn't break. Third, it was the Prophet's own last concern. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud records that among his last words, peace be upon him, was the prayer, the prayer, and care for those under your hand. Of all the things he could have left as final words, he pointed there. Fourth, look again at the history with that in mind. The prayer didn't depend on a caliph, so it didn't fall with one. A farmer's dawn prayer in a village never needed the court's permission. That's how a faith outlived its own empires, one person at a time, five times a day. And it's a lesson for any life that's going through its own rise and fall: a job ending, a move, an illness. The anchor that holds is the one that doesn't depend on the weather.
screen: `PRAYER AT FIXED HOURS, TIED TO THE SUN.` · `IN FEAR: STANDING OR ON HORSEBACK.` · `HIS LAST WORDS: THE PRAYER, THE PRAYER.` · `NO CALIPH NEEDED, SO NONE COULD END IT.` · then, large: `WORSHIP AT FIXED HOURS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray on time today. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself which prayer comes next, and roughly when. Look at the light through the window, if there is one. Is the sun high, slanting, low, gone? That light is the prayer's clock. If you pray, decide now exactly where you'll be when the next prayer comes, and how you'll step away to pray it on time. If you don't pray, choose that moment anyway, and when it comes, stop for one breath and notice the light. The bell holds the time.
The prayer never stopped. Empires rose and fell, and the five daily prayers, tied to the sun, went on through all of it. Today's word.
Your line: the prayer went on. Today, keep the moment you chose, and when the time comes, step away from whatever you're doing and pray or pause. Day one thousand fifty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims pray five times a day at times set by the sun (dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night); travelers may shorten some prayers, and the sick may pray sitting or lying down.

fork.setup: you're on a road in danger. you can't stop and dismount, and the time for prayer has come. what does the Qur'an say to do?
options: pray as you can, standing or on horseback.
wait until you're safe, however long it takes, and pray it late.
fork.reveal: Qur'an 2:239 says that in fear you pray standing or on horseback, and when you're safe again, you remember God as He taught you. the prayer bends; it doesn't stop.

original.note: Arabic: the ritual prayer, prayed five times a day.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prayer survived because powerful rulers enforced it.
what it means: the prayer was tied to the sun and to each person, so it went on when rulers fell.
what a scholar hears: 4:103's fixed hours, 2:239's prayer in fear, and the hadith in Abu Dawud placing the prayer among the Prophet's last words.

sources.quoted: Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:239 (in fear, pray standing or on horseback)
Qur'an 4:101 (shortening the prayer on a journey)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1117 (pray standing; if unable, sitting; if unable, on your side)
Sunan Abi Dawud 5156 (the prayer, the prayer, and those your right hands possess)

notes: Pickthall 4:103 fragment matches wording used elsewhere on this path; confirm. 2:239 paraphrased (Pickthall's wording not quoted).
Abu Dawud 5156 paraphrased; 'those your right hands possess' is rendered 'those under your hand'. Confirm number and the rendering.
Praying sitting or lying down when sick: Sahih al-Bukhari 1117 (Imran ibn Husayn), added to sources; confirm number.
Hook's list of fallen courts (Damascus, Baghdad, Cordoba, Cairo) is general, with no dates.
